Empirical Research Plan  
“Environmental Regulations, Pollution, and Infant Mortality in India”

========================================================
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------
Primary design:  Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event–study specification, implemented with the Callaway-Sant’Anna or Sun & Abraham estimators that are robust to heterogeneous treatment timing.

Why appropriate  
• Regulations rolled out across districts/states at different calendar dates ⇒ quasi-experimental variation in treatment timing.  
• Panel data on districts for ≥ 5 years before and after adoption ⇒ we can test for pre-trends and estimate dynamic effects.  
• Parallel-trends assumption is more credible than cross-sectional exogeneity because districts are compared to themselves over time.  

Second stage / causal chain:  Instrumental-Variables DID  
• Use the regulation-exposure dummy as an instrument for pollution when estimating the effect of pollution on infant mortality (2SLS within the DID framework).  
• This isolates exogenous variation in pollution stemming only from regulatory shocks, avoiding attenuation from measurement error and simultaneity.

========================================================
2. Treatment and Control Definition
--------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
T_it = 1 if district i is subject to the new environmental regulation in year t; 0 otherwise.

Control group  
District-years that have not yet adopted the regulation (or never adopt) serve as contemporaneous controls for each treated cohort.

Treatment timing  
For each district i, AdoptionYear_i is the first fiscal year in which the regulation legally binds (month or quarter can be used if available). Event time k = t – AdoptionYear_i.  

• k = 0: first year of enforcement  
• k < 0: pre-periods (leads)  
• k > 0: post-periods (lags)

No RDD running variable is used; the design is DID.

========================================================
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of the regulation, treated and not-yet-treated districts would have followed the same pollution/infant-mortality trends.  
Plausibility: Districts may differ systematically, but including district and year fixed effects, state-specific trends, and testing for pre-trends in the event study improves credibility.

A2. No Anticipatory Behavioral Response: Firms/households do not change pollution-related behavior before the official adoption year.  
Plausibility: Enforcement often begins only after notification; nevertheless, back-dating compliance is possible—checked via leads.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (No Spillovers): The regulation in one district does not directly change pollution or health outcomes in another (e.g., rivers cross districts, air plumes travel).  
Plausibility: More problematic for water; we will test for downstream/upwind spillovers and cluster at river-basin/air-shed level.

A4. Relevance of Instrument (for IV step): Regulation significantly reduces pollution.  
Plausibility: Supported by existing evidence and verified in first stage.

A5. Exclusion (for IV step): Regulation affects infant mortality only through pollution, not via other concurrent channels (e.g., income shocks).  
Plausibility: We will control for economic conditions, health spending, and run falsification tests on adult mortality.

========================================================
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
--------------------------------------------------------
Threat 1: Differential Pre-trends  
• Mitigation: Plot event-study coefficients for k = –5…–1; formally test that they are jointly zero.  
• Allow cohort-specific or state-specific linear trends as robustness.

Threat 2: Spillovers across districts (air shed / river basin).  
• Mitigation: (i) Include neighboring-district treatment share as a control.  
• (ii) Redefine treatment at the basin or air-shed level.  
• (iii) Cluster standard errors at that geographic unit.

Threat 3: Concurrent policies (e.g., health initiatives, economic shocks) adopted around same time.  
• Mitigation: Control for other major programs (NRHM, etc.); exclude years with national shocks; difference-out with district*year-of-birth fixed effects when using individual DHS micro-data.

========================================================
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------
```r
############################################
# 0. Packages
############################################
library(data.table)
library(fixest)          # fast FE regressions
library(did)             # Callaway & Sant’Anna
library(modelsummary)    # nice tables
library(sandwich)        # vcov
library(lmtest)          # coeftest

############################################
# 1. Data Loading & Merge
############################################
poll   <- fread("district_pollution.csv")    # yearly air & water measures
infant <- fread("district_infantmort.csv")   # IMR counts & births
reg    <- fread("regulation_adoption.csv")   # adoption year & enforcement score
controls <- fread("district_controls.csv")   # GDPpc, health infra, etc.

dt <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y,
             by = c("district_id","year"), all = TRUE),
             list(poll, infant, reg, controls))

############################################
# 2. Variable Construction
############################################
dt[, treat := as.integer(year >= adoption_year & !is.na(adoption_year))]
dt[, event_time := year - adoption_year]          # relative year
# pollution aggregates
dt[, log_pm25 := log(pm25 + 0.1)]
dt[, log_bod  := log(bod + 0.1)]                  # water
# infant mortality rate per 1,000 live births
dt[, imr := deaths_under1 / live_births * 1000]

############################################
# 3. Main DID (Callaway-Sant’Anna) – Effect on pollution
############################################
did_pm <- att_gt(yname   = "log_pm25",
                 tname   = "year",
                 idname  = "district_id",
                 gname   = "adoption_year",   # cohort
                 xformla = ~ gdp_pc + health_spend,
                 data    = dt)

agg_pm  <- aggte(did_pm, type = "dynamic")   # event study

############################################
# 4. 2SLS within DID – Effect on IMR
############################################
# First stage: pollution on treatment
fs <- feols(log_pm25 ~ treat | district_id + year,
            data = dt, cluster = "district_id")

# Second stage: IMR on predicted pollution using iv()
iv <- feols(imr ~ 1 | log_pm25 ~ treat |
            district_id + year,
            data = dt, cluster = "district_id")

############################################
# 5. Robustness: add state-specific linear trends
############################################
dt[, state_year := interaction(state_id, year)]
rob <- feols(log_pm25 ~ treat | district_id + year + state_id[year],
             data = dt, cluster = "district_id")

############################################
# 6. Output tables
############################################
modelsummary(list(DID_Pollution = fs,
                  IV_IMR = iv,
                  Robust = rob))
```

========================================================
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------
Economic priors:  
• Stringent environmental regulations should lower ambient PM2.5 and BOD levels.  
• Literature from China and Latin America suggests 5–15 % declines in targeted pollutants within 3 years.  
• Infant mortality is elastic with respect to air pollution; a 10 µg/m³ fall in PM2.5 is often associated with a 3–5 % fall in IMR.  

Thus, I anticipate:  
(i) log(PM2.5) ↓ 7–10 % within five years of adoption.  
(ii) IMR ↓ 2–4 deaths per 1,000 live births (~5 % of the sample mean).

========================================================
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID)
--------------------------------------------------------
C1: Credible parallel trends (tested & backed by pre-trends) ………………… 0.8  
C2: No interference/spillovers between units ……………………………………… 0.6  
C3: No anticipation (pre-treatment behavior) ……………………………………… 0.7  
C4: Correct treatment timing & no misclassification ……………………………… 0.9  
C5: Robust standard errors & inference suited to design ……………………… 1.0  

Average score ≈ 0.8 ⇒ reasonably strong but not perfect identification.

========================================================
End of Plan
